title: Beam Routing through Excitons in Transition Metal Dichalcogenide Monolayers
authors: Yonas Lebsir, Jacob Terndrup Heiden, Jorge Barcia Rodríguez, Maria Papadopoulou, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, N. Asger Mortensen, Sergii Morozov, Nicolas Ubrig
abstract: Routing light at the nanoscale typically relies on nanostructured surfaces to imprint directionality on the emission. Using low-temperature, angle-resolved cathodoluminescence spectroscopy, we show that the intrinsic excitonic transitions of a semiconductor can themselves produce routed emission. We probe monolayers of WSe$_2$, MoSe$_2$, and MoTe$_2$ and resolve the excitonic species of monolayer WSe$_2$ -- the bright exciton, the trion, and the spin-forbidden dark exciton -- through their distinct angular emission profiles. While the in-plane transition dipoles of the bright exciton and trion radiate predominantly toward the surface normal, the out-of-plane dipole of the dark exciton, inaccessible under normal-incidence optical excitation, produces a directional emission channel at large angles. We further tune the balance between neutral and charged exciton emission through the local dielectric environment. Our results establish dark excitons in TMD monolayers as a platform for directional light emission in compact photonic architectures without additional nanostructuring.
summary: The research shows that light beam routing at the nanoscale can be achieved intrinsically within TMD monolayers without needing external nanostructures. By using angle-resolved cathodoluminescence, the authors prove that the dark exciton possesses an out-of-plane dipole moment, causing it to emit directionally at large angles relative to the surface normal.
main_problem: To achieve nanoscale beam routing of light without relying on external nanostructuring elements.
main_result: The intrinsic excitonic transitions within TMD monolayers, particularly the dark exciton, can produce highly directional emission channels at large angles.
method: Low-temperature, angle-resolved cathodoluminescence spectroscopy is used to probe and distinguish between different excitonic species based on their angular emission profiles.
model_or_system: The study focuses on monolayer Transition Metal Dichalcogenides ($	ext{WSe}_2$, $	ext{MoSe}_2$, $	ext{MoTe}_2$), which host distinct excitonic species: bright exciton, trion, and dark exciton. These species possess different transition dipole orientations (in-plane vs. out-of-plane).
key_observables: Emission energy, emission angle ($	heta$), and the relative intensity of $	ext{X}^0$, $	ext{X}_T$, and $	ext{X}_D$ as a function of collection angle.
important_parameters: Low temperature (down to 83 K), local dielectric environment, and the presence/thickness of encapsulating layers like hBN or graphene.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the distinct angular emission profiles are solely determined by the orientation of the respective excitonic transition dipoles.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the experimental setup, band diagrams, and measured spectra showing how $	ext{X}_D$ appears at large angles due to its out-of-plane dipole, while $	ext{X}^0$ and $	ext{X}_T$ peak near the surface normal.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem of nanoscale light routing, details the use of TMDs with multiple excitonic species, presents experimental measurements using angle-resolved CL to map out dipole orientations, and concludes that intrinsic material properties can achieve directional emission.
why_interesting: This work demonstrates a solid-state platform for controlling photon emission directionality purely through quantum mechanical selection rules (dipole orientation), which is highly relevant for integrated photonic devices and open quantum systems engineering.
